newsitem.title: UK: U.S. Treasuries flat in London, await data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries flat in London, await data.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries in London hovered around unchanged levels on Friday as investors stayed cautious ahead of economic data which could weigh on prices near-term, analysts said.
Activity was paltry and traders said any technical bounce was likely to be short-lived before first quarter U.S. GDP at 1230 GMT and a University of Michigan consumer confidence survey at 1400 GMT.
Also, sentiment was nervous ahead of the Federal Reserve's two-day meeting on Tuesday on interest rates, and a week laden with crucial data including June payrolls, traders said.

"Some quarter-end buying will help on the margins, but news of a soft economy is behind us and the data will begin to look mixed or stronger," said Charles Quigley, U.S. bond salesman at Chase in London.
"We'll struggle in the short-term to do much better. I can't see that much advertises well for the Treasury market," he added.

By 1030 GMT, the benchmark long bond was quoted at 98-05, yielding 6.77 percent, compared with 98-04 in Tokyo. A bout of profit-taking in New York had shaved 17/32 off Treasuries to close at 98-00 on Thursday.
A Reuter poll of economists forecast U.S. Q1 final GDP data to show a 5.9 percent increase, versus 5.8 percent previously.
But economists said the market's spotlight would be more on the Michigan report, which a Reuter poll forecast at a slightly higher 103.5 from 103.2 previously.
"The risk is the report will be revised up slightly," said Rob Hayward, U.S. economist at BankAmerica.
"It will keep the market cautious about the risk consumer spending will rise in the second half of the year."
Recent data has pointed to a slowdown in the pace of U.S. growth after a rapid rise in the first quarter. This has cooled speculation about a Fed rate rise.
Hayward said a hike was unlikely next week, even if the Michigan report was strong, but said there remained a risk the Fed would pull the trigger later in the year.
"If consumer spending is up, there still remains some risk the Fed will have to do something in the second half of the year," Hayward added.
September T-bond futures were 5/32 higher at 111-10 in automated trade.
